article_text: Ben Needham's mum Kerry warns Greek locals she 'isn't going anywhere' as she dismisses claim her son is dead in new Disney+ crime documentary Kerry believes Ben is still alive Kerry Needham, the mother of missing toddler Ben, has issued a stark warning to the residents of Kos in a brand new Disney+ documentary. The bereft mum and her own mother – Ben’s grandmother – appear in the streaming service’s new series 20/20 Britain’s Most Notorious Crime Investigations. And she is very quick to dismiss the police’s previous conclusion that Ben died in Greece aged 21 months. Kerry has said that without a body or remains there is no evidence that Ben, who vanished in 1991, is dead. Ben Needham: Lost in Paradise on Disney+ 20/20 Britain’s Most Notorious Crime Investigations dropped today (Thursday July 30, 2026) on Disney+. The episode about little Ben is the first in the six-part series. Called Ben Needham: Lost in Paradise, the documentary looks back at the lead up to Ben’s disappearance in Kos, and what has happened since. Kerry and her mum Christine explain the story right from the start. And it begins with Kerry returning to Kos last year. Looking out to sea, she admits: “I hate coming back here. It makes me shake, it makes me feel physically sick. Coming back here makes me relive that day.” The family had left a “very poor area” in Sheffield, England, and moved to Kos in the early 90s. Kerry has two brothers, Stephen and Danny, who initially relocated with Christine and their dad Eddie. Kerry stayed in England with Ben’s dad Simon Ward. But their flat was dingy, they were young and Kerry missed her family. So she and Ben moved out to Kos, too. The family had rented an olive grove and Eddie and Stephen began working on the renovation of a farmhouse nearby. Kerry got a job in a local hotel bar as a waitress, while Christine looked after Ben. On that fateful day, Christine and Ben headed to visit Eddie and Stephen at work. Ben was playing with his two Dinky toy cars outside the farmhouse door. But a short while later, Christine was unable to find him. “Eddie went across the field shouting his name but he wasn’t there,” Christine recalls in the documentary. Stephen had already left on his motorbike to go home for a shower. Assumptions he had taken Ben with him were wrong. Christine and Stephen went to the local police station to report Ben missing, though no one could find him. As viewers of Ben Needham: Lost in Paradise will see, what ensued has been almost a four-decade hunt for Kerry’s beloved son. What happened to Ben Needham? In their search for Ben, Kerry and Christine reveal how they were sent on a wild goose chase. A public appeal on a Greek television programme sparked a call from a prisoner in jail. The man insisted a local Roma traveller family had stolen Ben. Christine and Eddie tracked them down with an interpreter but they were met with vitriol from the community. Shock scenes in Ben’s episode of 20/20 Britain’s Most Notorious Crime Investigations show a man hiding something under a tea towel. He screams and threatens to shoot them dead. There have been hundreds of reports of sightings of Ben since 1991. Computer generated images have provided age progression pictures but he has never been found. In 2012, South Yorkshire Police launched a new inquiry into Ben’s disappearance. Officers returned to Kos and spent years conducting a full scale dig and investigation in the area where he vanished. Officers concluded that Ben died in a digger accident. Did Konstantinos ‘Dino’ Barkas kill Ben Needham? Four years after the inquiry was launched, the police made a breakthrough. A witness claimed Ben had been playing close to where digger driver Konstantinos ‘Dino’ Barkas was driving his massive piece of machinery. The witness said he saw Dino on the following days and said he was “red, upset and sweating and in quite a state”. Detective Superintendent Matt Fenwick adds in the Disney+ documentary: “Dino said, ‘I ran over something that yelped and I thought it was a dog’.” Dino, who died in 2015, was said to have buried Ben’s body that same day. An excavation of an olive grove later recovered one of Ben’s Dinky cars. Forensic evidence on the toy car found it had been in contact with blood or tissue that had decomposed. DS Fenwick says: “You’re left with the one plausible explanation. I think that Dino went into the area where Eddie was doing the renovation. Ben was playing between the two properties. “I think it’s likely that Ben came onto contact with that huge piece of machinery. I think Ben died as a result of that.” DS confirms in the documentary that believes it was an accident. He thinks Ben’s body was moved by Dino in a bid to cover up his crime. Dino’s family, however, vehemently deny South Yorkshire Police’s theory. And there’s a twist. Kerry Needham issues warning to Kos locals Two years after the car was found, Kerry received a phone call. It came following advances in DNA testing. She tearfully recalls in the Disney+ documentary: “They said, ‘Kerry, I’m sorry to tell you but the human decomposition inside the car, it’s not a match to Ben’s’. “I was thinking, why are you sorry? Because that means he’s alive. It means the accident didn’t happen. “You didn’t find his body or anything else. All you found was a toy car. So he’s not dead then.” Kerry vows to never stop looking for her little boy. In a very stark warning to the people of Kos, she says: “Ben is still a missing person in my mind. We as a family will never let this lie. “I appeal to those people on Kos to tell me the truth, tell me what happened. Tell me where he is if you can and I will go away. “But until then, I’m not going anywhere.”

John Kennedy has admitted that President Donald Trump’s push to prosecute vandals for damage to his newly renovated Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool may have been a political ploy. “This is a case that the DOJ said was open and shut. They could prove it without reasonable doubt,” host Kristen Welker said on Meet the Press Sunday, after charges against former Olympian David Hearn were dropped. With the Trump administration now conceding a “botched” repair job, Kennedy, 74, admitted: “Well, the whole thing is a multiple vehicle pileup.” He then said of Trump’s vandalism conspiracy: “Let me start with the president. The president says it was caused by vandals. I don’t know whether he really believes that or it’s part of his political messaging or he’s just thinking out loud.” Kennedy said of his boss: “You and I both know the president well. He exists loudly and he grows anxious when he has an unexpressed thought. “I’m not saying he doesn’t really believe it, I just don’t know.” The attorney offered a similar assessment on Jeanine Pirro, who had initially backed Trump’s assertion that vandals were to blame for the Reflecting Pool fiasco before backtracking on Friday. “The stakes are a lot higher for U.S. Attorney Pirro. You can’t lie to a federal judge,” he said. “If she can’t prove her case, she was right to pull back. Because if you fool around with a federal judge, you will find out.” In classic Kennedy form, the senator used a bizarre anecdote to illustrate his point. “When I was in private practice one time, I put my briefcase on a brand new conference table bought by a federal judge,” he said. “And he got so mad, I’ll never forget, I thought I was going to get to spend overnight with bubba in central lockup.” Getting back to the matter at hand, Kennedy mused: “Federal judges will not tolerate—and so if—I don’t know why she filed a suit without doing a full investigation. “She says she relied on the Department of the Interior, but she was smart to pull it back.” Before being discharged pre-trial, Hearn could have faced up to a decade behind bars for his alleged tampering with the pool. article_text: Georgia man who ran toward Capitol with shotgun pleads guilty (CBS NEWS) – Sources from CBS News say that a Georgia man who charged at the U.S. Capitol armed with a loaded shotgun and wearing body armor and camouflage clothing pleaded guilty on Monday to illegally carrying a firearm, court records show. Carter Camacho, 18, of Smyrna, Georgia, told police officers who apprehended him outside the Capitol on Feb. 17 that he intended to confront members of Congress and “scare them into speaking the truth,” according to federal prosecutors. But he didn’t make it into the building, and nobody was injured. Camacho is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. 8 by U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, D.C. He has remained jailed since his arrest. Camacho pleaded guilty to two counts: illegal possession of a firearm on Capitol grounds and receipt or distribution of child pornography. The latter charge stems from a search of his phone after his arrest. Surveillance video captured Camacho exiting a parked car and running toward the west side of the Capitol, the side that is adjacent to the National Mall, with the shotgun in his hands. He complied with Capitol Police officers’ commands to stop and get down on the ground. “This individual was challenged by United States Capitol Police officers in order to drop the weapon, which he did comply with,” U.S. Capitol Police Chief Michael Sullivan said in February. Sullivan had said the man, whom he didn’t name at the time, was wearing a tactical vest and had tactical gloves. He said the shotgun was loaded, and the man was carrying additional rounds. Officers found a Kevlar helmet and a gas mask in his vehicle, Sullivan said. Camacho told police that he purchased the shotgun for “home defense” less than a week before he drove from Georgia to the Capitol, prosecutors said. He also said he had left pepper spray and other tactical gear in his car “just in case I don’t want to shoot anyone,” according to prosecutors. “He further indicated that he considered using the shotgun to breach a door to be able to enter the Capitol,” they wrote.

article_text: By Tarek Anthony oregonlive.com SALEM, Ore. — More than 1 million acres continued to burn across Oregon on Tuesday as firefighters took advantage of a rare stretch of thunderstorm-free weather to battle dozens of active wildfires across the state. | BETTER EVERY SHIFT: Fennessy’s vision for the future of wildfire response Here is an update on the largest fires burning statewide: Bench fire The Bench and Beachcomb fires merged into a single, fast-growing blaze that had burned more than 45,000 acres on the Warm Springs Indian Reservation in central Oregon by Tuesday. The fire destroyed six homes and five other structures Sunday night into Monday, fueled by strong winds, officials said. Strong winds Monday pushed the fire across both sides of the Deschutes River and Lake Billy Chinook, driving it toward more populated areas and threatening multiple communities on the Warm Springs Reservation. Level 3 (go now)evacuation orders remain in effect across much of the reservation north of Lake Billy Chinook and west of Madras. Officials have opened shelters for residents at the Old School Cafeteria in Warm Springs and St. Patrick Catholic School in Madras. A large-animal shelter remains open at the Jefferson County Fairgrounds in Madras. Pacific Power shut off electricity at three locations on the reservation, affecting fewer than 50 residents. Crews battled 90-degree heat and strong winds Monday as officials warned there was a “high potential” for further fire growth. Rowe Creek complex More than 1,300 personnel are battling the Rowe Creek complex, which encompasses nearly a dozen fires across central Oregon and is anchored by the roughly 71,000-acre fire formerly known as the Brewer fire east of Madras. The Brewer fire merged Monday with the Green Mountain and Crosswhite fires, bringing the combined burn area to more than 294,000 acres. The merged blaze is now known as the Rowe Creek complex-west zone. Officials have closed more than 20 miles of U.S. 26 east of Prineville, from milepost 34.8 to milepost 66, because of fire activity. The highway is a key route connecting Prineville and John Day and beyond into Idaho. Crews are focused on protecting homes east of Prineville, including in the Mill Creek, Johnson Creek and Marks Creek areas. Evacuation orders remain in effect across large portions of Crook and Jefferson counties, though relatively few residents are affected. Operations Chief Rob Hutchens said crews received two additional firefighting crews from California on Tuesday morning as firefighters continued efforts to protect homes along the southern edge of the fire. Air quality also remained a concern across the Prineville area Tuesday with Air Quality Index readings measuring at 152 out of 500 — considered to be unhealthy for sensitive groups. The blaze is 33% contained. Akawa Butte fire The lightning-caused Akawa Butte fire continues to burn more than 27,000 acres north of Sisters. Despite hot, breezy conditions Monday, crews made progress extinguishing hot spots and clearing lingering heat up to 100 feet inside the fire line. Operations Chief Cody Lokan said Tuesday morning that crews had contained the northeastern corner of the fire, which had been burning on remote public land. Operations Chief Steve Chapman said crews would remain focused Tuesday on cleaning up burned material in the fire’s southwestern area, where homes are most concentrated. Chapman said firefighters use water and hand tools to mix burning material into what crews call a “mud pie” to ensure it does not reignite. “It’s kind of like being a kid sometimes, so it’s kind of fun,” Chapman said. Oregon State Fire Marshal teams will spend their last night on the fire Tuesday, Chapman said, as crews begin transitioning cleanup efforts back to wildland firefighters. Officials will hold a community meeting at Sisters High School at 6:30 p.m. Tuesday to provide residents with the latest updates. Power remains shut off along Wilt Road northeast of Sisters to ensure firefighter safety. Shelters remain open at Sisters High School for evacuees and at Pole Creek Ranch for large animals. The fire is 6% contained. Big Grass fire Oregon’s largest wildfire, the Big Grass fire, has burned more than 300,000 acres across eastern Malheur County and into southwestern Idaho. Level 3 (go now) evacuation orders remain in effect for the Pleasant Valley, South Mountain and Jordan Valley areas. The fire is burning primarily on sparsely populated Bureau of Land Management land in the Owyhee region, limiting its impact on homes and communities. Harney County In southeast Oregon, the Second Flat fire has burned nearly 92,500 acres east of Burns in Harney County. Because the fire is burning in a sparsely populated area, evacuation orders affect relatively few residents. Air quality remains unhealthy, however, with Air Quality Index readings reaching 187 on Tuesday. Residents are encouraged to avoid outdoor activities and keep doors and windows closed to prevent smoke from entering their homes. Elsewhere in Harney County, the Jackass and Bald Mountain fires have collectively burned about 54,000 acres as of Tuesday and remain largely uncontained. The Coleman Creek fire, which spans eastern Harney County and western Malheur County, has burned more than 146,000 acres. A shelter for residents affected by the Coleman Creek fire has been established at Crane Union High School. Hagen fire The Hagen fire in Umatilla County continues to cause unhealthy air quality across Pendleton and much of northeast Oregon. The blaze had burned nearly 30,000 acres east of the Umatilla Indian Reservation as of Tuesday, with evacuation orders remaining in place across the area. Though Level 3 (go now) evacuation orders affect few residents, an evacuation shelter has been established at Sunridge Middle School in Pendleton, where Air Quality Index readings reached 154 out of 500 on Tuesday, a level considered unhealthy. Residents are encouraged to limit time outdoors and keep windows and doors closed to prevent smoke from entering their homes. Powder River, Fox and Tartar fires Areas of eastern Oregon near Baker City remain blanketed in heavy smoke and hazardous air as three nearby fires continue to burn. The Powder River fire, the oldest of the three, has burned more than 21,000 acres near Richland and was 84% contained Tuesday. Crews have benefited from several days without severe thunderstorms and continue cleanup operations in the area. South of the Powder River fire, the Fox fire has burned more than 58,000 acres along the Snake River and the Idaho border, becoming authorities’ main priority in the area. The blaze prompted the closure of 80 miles of Interstate 84 on Monday because of dangerous conditions, though the highway has since reopened. Officials said Tuesday that winds are again expected to push smoke and fire activity toward the interstate and urged motorists to slow down as firefighters work along the roadway. Across the Snake River in western Idaho, the Tartar fire had burned 12,100 acres as of Tuesday and was 15% contained. Air quality in Baker City measured 157 on the Air Quality Index on Tuesday, a level considered unhealthy. Ontario recorded some of the state’s worst air quality, with a reading of 195. Residents are encouraged to limit time outdoors and keep windows and doors closed to prevent smoke from entering homes. More than 150 residents remain without power after Idaho Power shut off electrical lines to reduce the risk of additional fires. Hay Creek complex The Hay Creek complex, which encompasses numerous fires burning across north-central Oregon, is now 90% contained after burning more than 193,000 acres. The largest fire in the complex, the Hoag fire, burned about 50,000 acres along the John Day River in Sherman County but is now 100% contained. article_text: The Ministry of National Defense yesterday said it is monitoring the construction of full-scale replicas of military and government sites in Taiwan by the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA). The comments from ministry spokesman Major General Sun Li-fang (孫立方) come after a report by the Telegraph on satellite imagery showing replicas of Taiwan’s Presidential Office Building, Suao Naval Base and other sites. Citing satellite imagery and defense analysts, the report, published on Sunday, said that the PLA had built life-size replicas of key government facilities to rehearse military operations under realistic conditions. Photo: Screen grab from Google Earth The report described the scale and specificity of the training facilities as “unprecedented.” China had constructed replicas of Yokosuka Naval Base in Japan, which has the largest US naval base in that country, and Suao Naval Base in Yilan County, it said. Satellite imagery showed a mock-up of a Keelung-class destroyer berthed inside the replica of the Suao base, it said. Reports of PLA mock-up facilities have surfaced several times in the past few years. Satellite imagery first showed replicas of US aircraft carriers and destroyers in China’s northwestern deserts in 2021, while analysts in 2024 identified life-size replicas of Taipei’s Boai Special Zone, including the Presidential Office Building, at a military base in Inner Mongolia. More recent imagery has shown mock-ups of the Suao base and the Yokosuka base, which analysts say could be used to rehearse strikes against key military and government targets in a Taiwan contingency. Asked about the report, Sun said the military has “a comprehensive understanding” of the PLA’s construction of the replicas through its intelligence-gathering efforts. The armed forces have consistently planned for all possible scenarios involving Chinese military action against Taiwan and developed contingency measures, he said. “The disclosure of this information reminds us that the threats we face today are extremely serious,” Sun said, adding that the ministry takes the developments seriously and would continue strengthening force development, combat readiness and military training. article_text: Published July 29, 2026 RAWALAKOT: Law enforcement agencies continue operations against armed groups carrying out attacks against security personnel in Azad Jammu and Kashmir's (AJK) Rawalakot, a top police official said on Wednesday. Addressing a press conference in Rawalakot, AJK police spokesperson, Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Khawar Ali Shaukat, said that armed attackers have taken positions in different buildings across the city. His remarks come amid violent clashes in the city involving supporters of the proscribed Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) amid general elections in the region. The AJK government had declared JAAC a proscribed organisation on June 5 under the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA), accusing the group of involvement in terrorism. The ban was imposed days before the committee's planned June 9 protest demanding the abolition of 12 AJK Assembly seats reserved for refugees from Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir (IIOJK) who migrated to Pakistan after 1947. During today's presser, SSP Shaukat said that armed groups continue carrying out attacks on law enforcement personnel in different areas, adding that no concession would be given to "miscreant elements". According to the official, at least one Rangers personnel was martyred in the attacks as enforcement agencies continue operations against the armed groups. The AJK police spokesperson said that police arrested several miscreants during the ongoing operations and recovered sophisticated weapons. Terming the attacks on security forces and state institutions "unacceptable", he maintained that state institutions had consistently exercised restraint. Those involved in attacks against state institutions would be dealt with "with an iron hand", he said. SSP Shaukat said that the "links" of the miscreants extended elsewhere and claimed that anti-state elements were spreading negative propaganda on social media. He vowed that authorities would not allow peace in the region to be undermined. The federal government has termed the violence involving the banned JAAC an attempt to disrupt the ongoing electoral process and undermine peace in the region. State Minister for Interior Talal Chaudhry on Tuesday said that the federal government would fully support the AJK administration to crush agitators. Speaking at a press conference in Islamabad alongside Federal Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, the minister said that the banned outfit's campaign was "not a movement to secure rights, but one aimed at taking rights away from the people". He alleged that the proscribed group was seeking to deprive Kashmiris of their right to vote and undermine the democratic process. The first phase of the AJK elections was held on July 27, with Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) securing victory in nine constituencies, according to unofficial and provisional results. Polling was held across all 13 constituencies in Mirpur, Kotli and Bhimber districts. According to the unofficial results, the PML-N won nine seats, while the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) secured four.

The landing site was discovered by Polish authorities alongside scattered debris after reports of an explosion near the south-east village of Tarnawa-Kolonia. Fighter jets were scrambled, but Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said there was no immediate danger as the missile fell in an uninhabited area. Local authorities said the farmland where the crater was found is around 1.2 miles from the nearest residential buildings. Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X: ‘Overnight, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crossed into Poland as part of Russia’s massive strike against Ukraine, violating NATO airspace.’ Tusk said the object ‘looks like’ a Russian missile but authorities did not have ‘100% certainty’ what kind of missile it was. article_text: Decaying bodies found at funeral home 'horror scene' as boss is sentenced - and one family 'given ashes in Hobbycraft bag' Robert Bush, who ran Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, even kept the remains of a stillborn baby in an envelope on the cold room floor for almost two years Want LBC stories before everyone else? Set us as your Preferred Source on Google Warning: This story contains distressing content A funeral boss who gave families the wrong ashes and kept bodies on stretchers on the floor in filthy storage boxes is being sentenced from today in front of the horrified loved ones of those whose bodies he mishandled. Listen to this article Robert Bush, who ran Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, will be sentenced from today after pleading guilty to 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial. The 48-year-old gave grieving families the wrong ashes while their loved ones’ bodies were left at his site for months. His offences spanned 12 years and affected hundreds of victims. Emotional victim impact statements which spoke of the "pain and grief" inflicted by the "cruelty" of Bush were shared by loved ones of the deceased on Monday. The family of 64-year-old Colin Wainman were given his ashes "inside a Hobbycraft bag", because Bush "did not have any gift bags left". Read more: 'Monster' funeral director admits preventing 30 burials and stealing money from mourners The family-owned Hull business became the centre of a criminal investigation after police were contacted by someone with access to the site in March 2024, expressing concerns over “care of the deceased". When officers searched the premises, they found 31 bodies that should have been cremated months earlier, including a stillborn baby that had been there for almost two years. They also found more than 100 sets of ashes, some with name labels and letters attached to the box. The mother of one stillborn baby has described her distress after a funeral director kept his remains in an envelope on the cold room floor for almost two years. Jasmine Beverley was one of hundreds of victims of funeral director Robert Bush, who is being sentenced at Hull Crown Court after breaching the trust of grieving families. Her son, Sunny, was born stillborn at about 18 weeks and she believed he had been given a funeral and cremated.But, instead, his tiny remains lay on the floor of the Legacy Independent Funeral Directors premises, kept in what looked to a police officer to resemble an evidence bag. Chris Paxton KC, prosecuting, told the court: "In this bag was a white cotton pad.“It looked like a dressing-type pad used by hospitals. "[The officer] opened the pad and inside was a tiny item which he initially thought was a baby bird.“Although initially unsure, he suspected it was a human foetus." Norman Bridger's body was left in a cardboard coffin on Legacy premises for 10 months after his death, which his daughter described as "beyond belief". Karen King, the 94-year-old's daughter, said her "lovely dad" was still wearing the grey T-shirt in which he had died. She told the court: “My lovely dad lay in a cardboard coffin for almost 11 months. It is beyond belief." When police informed Karen of the situation, she "broke down in tears", telling the court: "How could someone be so cruel? Why would he just leave him there?”. The fraudulent funeral director reportedly showed no emotion whilst listening from the dock. The body of 73-year-old Jonathan Butler was left on Legacy premises for eight months. His partner, Kathryn Howard, was visibly emotional and struggled to get through her statement in court. She said an apology from Bush would not be enough, and "could never take away the pain and grief that I feel for enduring not one, but two, funerals for my lovely John. "I wouldn’t wish it on anyone," she added. Muriel Winning's body was kept on the property for seven months after her death. The son of the 61-year-old, Byron Lill, had been given ashes that he believed belonged to his mother, which he kept on his windowsill. He said his family had taken "tireless" care to prepare Muriel in her wedding dress, "in readiness for meeting with (her husband) David again" - efforts which he said were "for nothing". The loved ones of 64-year-old Raymond Dagnall were also given ashes that they believed belonged to Raymond - only to later discover that there had been no cremation, despite Bush charging them for one. Raymond's sister, Christina George, sobbed as she told the court: "I will never forgive Bush for his neglect and complete lack of respect." “I try and think of all the good memories I have of us growing up as children together, but I keep coming back in my mind to him laying forgotten on a rack. Police found that many families of the deceased found at Legacy had already been given ashes by Bush, revealing a widespread practice of him giving grieving relatives the wrong ashes. Investigators also learned that Bush had committed fraudulent trading in relation to funeral plans, where he would take payment for the plans but not pass any of the money on to the financial institutions that would hold it for when the funeral was required. He also stole from charities by failing to pass on donations collected at funerals. In April, Bush pleaded guilty to 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial, and theft from 12 charities including the Salvation Army and Macmillan Cancer Support. He had already admitted 30 counts of fraud by false representation relating to bodies found at the site, and four “foetus allegations” of fraud, where he presented ashes to women falsely saying that they were “the remains of their unborn”. Bush also pleaded guilty to a further charge of fraud, covering the ashes of 57 people between 2017 and 2024, and one of fraudulent trading relating to funeral plans between 2012 and 2024.

article_text: ALLEN TWP., Pa. -- The Philadelphia Police Commissioner is responding to the arrest of one of his officers for a shooting in Northampton County. That officer was off duty at the time, and he's now charged with homicide in the killing of his own uncle. It was just before 2 p.m. Friday when shots rang out in a house on Old Gate Rd. in Allen Township. 25-year-old Philadelphia Police Officer Kenroy Cummings is accused of shooting and killing his own uncle, 27-year-old Shakair Moncrieffe. The police report said one of Cummings' younger relatives called him to the house because Moncrieffe was threatening the boy. It was a shock to John Sousa and Jerry Caliendo, who live on the same street. "I was at work at the time, and my daughter texted me because she heard about it. Then my other daughter texted me to make sure I was alright, see if I was home," said Sousa. "They roped off the whole area for the day and the next day, when nobody could get their car out," said Caliendo. It was also shocking for Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel. "It's a tragedy when we have a police officer taking the life of someone, and so we're investigating that matter," said Bethel. Investigating how a respected member of the force for several years got involved in something like this. "Two years, from all indications I get, he was a good police officer here," said Bethel. "We train our men and women in deescalation. We train our men and women not to use deadly force." But Cummings admitted to using deadly force on his uncle, shooting him six times in the head and once in the wrist, according to court records. Cummings told police it was self-defense, because Moncrieffe was going for Cummings' gun, but Bethel said whatever the backstory is, it will likely end with Cummings losing his badge. "Over the next period of time, we'll go through a process where we will start to move him and remove him from the police department. Dismiss him from the police department," said Bethel. It's a story Sousa is still trying to fully understand. "A cop being involved in something like this? I mean that's crazy. You look to those people to protect and serve, not to perpetrate something like this," said Sousa.

article_text: NEW YORK – Farah Berent, a physician assistant in Holland, Michigan, used to learn about politics from channels like ABC, CBS and CNN. But that changed as she decided that coverage of the war in Gaza was irreparably biased. "I couldn’t stand all the lies on the stations,″ said Berent, arguing that there wasn't enough attention being paid to Palestinian suffering. "I started going to Instagram to get my news.” Recommended Videos Berent is among many progressive-minded Americans who have sworn off legacy media institutions. They're turning to a widening mix of independent podcasts, social media accounts and digital news sites, part of an increasingly influential ecosystem that has boosted this year's wave of anti-establishment, left-leaning candidates who may not have gotten as much attention otherwise. Liberals remain more likely than conservatives to trust mainstream outlets, but the splintering echoes how conservatives skeptical of their party created a collection of insurgent news sites years ago. The shift has elevated individual commentators with opinions on the news, some of whom have proven influential in driving people’s votes. Ryan Grim, a co-founder of Drop Site News and a veteran of online political debates, said progressive politicians have sought out his platform to reach voters. In a change from previous election cycles, "they have ways to get covered even if the mainstream just basically ignores them,” he said. One of those candidates is Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for U.S. Senate in Michigan and faces the more moderate U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in the Aug 4. primary. “I think in a lot of ways, where traditional media has been gatekeepers, we’re watching that gatekeeping function fall away,” El-Sayed said. Anti-establishment media has exploded lately These changes have been on display this year in places like New York City, where a slate of progressive congressional candidates endorsed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani defeated establishment-backed candidates. Sara Hyler, a policy analyst in East Harlem, originally planned to support incumbent Rep. Adriano Espaillat in last month's Democratic primary. But then Hyler started learning about progressive outsider Darializa Avila Chevalier through YouTube videos and podcasts, including from the liberal media company MeidasTouch. “My actual beliefs are to the left of Democrats. I don't want a moderate,” said Hyler, who ultimately voted for Avila Chevalier in hopes she could help nudge Congress toward progressive policies. The rise of independent media has been part of a digital transformation that transcends politics, as chronically online Americans are turning toward news from social media and content creators. But it's not just the popularity of smartphones driving that change. “There’s a complete lack of trust in any and all institutions now,” said Mike Nellis, a Democratic consultant who hosts a podcast, writes a Substack and posts political analysis on social media. “That has led people to turn to individuals, and so now you’re picking your flavor of person to listen to.” Among conservatives, faith in mainstream media and in the more moderate wing of the Republican Party faltered years ago, with the rise of the Tea Party movement paving the way for an alternative right-wing media ecosystem, including sites like the Daily Caller, Breitbart and The Blaze. Trump also tapped into a loose constellation of podcasts, including "The Joe Rogan Experience," for his successful comeback campaign. Reece Peck, a media culture professor at the College of Staten Island, said the left-wing version of that has happened slowly, beginning with the momentum of Sen. Bernie Sanders’ first presidential run in 2016. At the time, left-wing, anti-establishment YouTube accounts and podcasts like “The Young Turks” and “Chapo Trap House” were gaining attention but didn't reach the majority of Democratic voters. Now Democrats have realized their faith in institutions didn't prevent Trump's return. “The ground has been made fertile for an anti-establishment media politics, where it just wasn’t quite there with the voter base in those previous cycles,” Peck said. Even older, moderate liberals, he said, have started to ″throw their hands in the air and look for alternatives.” YouTube accounts like ”Secular Talk" and “Breaking Points,” streamers like Hasan Piker and new digital journalism organizations like More Perfect Union and The Lever are among those that have seen their audiences multiply. Grim said Drop Site has amassed 800,000 free and 60,000 paid subscribers since launching two years ago — more than he'd anticipated. Saul Levin, a Michigan progressive organizer who recently started his own podcast about artificial intelligence data centers, said Trump’s attacks on the existing media landscape are part of the reason for that growth. “The investigations and raids on numerous different journalists, the appointment of specifically aligned billionaires to lead various major news agencies, is very troubling,” he said. “Creators and new media outlets are stepping in and trying to fill gaps.” Alternative media is prominent in the Michigan primary The Michigan primary will be the latest test of the evolving media ecosystem, which El-Sayed, a longtime podcaster himself, has tried to harness. Various progressive outlets, creators and organizers have aggressively promoted his campaign. El-Sayed said the rise of independent media has let voters compare news across different channels and notice biases, but he doesn't turn down opportunities on legacy media, either. “I go on Fox News, I go on podcasts, I Twitch stream, we have a YouTube channel,” he said. Stevens, who received endorsements from outgoing incumbent Sen. Gary Peters, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, has a more traditional approach. She's also backed by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, and its affiliated groups, which have spent close to $30 million on the race. Stevens' campaign declined to comment for this story. Reporting from progressive outlets has influenced how the race has unfolded. For example, Stevens parted ways with a campaign consultant when Drop Site revealed that she had also worked for tech company Palantir, which is controversial in liberal circles because of its government contracts involving immigration enforcement. Democratic officials said Trump's return to the White House has also revived interest in the party's official channels. The Democratic National Committee's relatively new digital media offering, a rapid-response clipping and messaging account with the handle @FactPostNews, has amassed more than 2 billion impressions on Threads, X, Facebook, Instagram and Bluesky in 2026 alone. “I remember thinking to myself, there’s a chance that this flops and doesn’t get any traction,” said DNC Deputy Chief Mobilization Officer Paulina Mangubat. “It's been really, really successful.” At times, the mix of new voices on the left has erupted in public tensions. Grim recently faced criticism for boosting failed Democratic candidate Graham Platner in Maine, and he was accused of trying to undermine the credibility of the sexual assault allegation that torpedoed Platner's campaign. Grim said while he recognized people were angry, his reporting on the allegation was meant to share additional context. “If we’re going to litigate allegations in the court of public opinion, we can’t pick and choose what details we want to share with the public out of a fear of how they’ll be received,” he said. More recently, when Drop Site interviewed progressive U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna of California, one of its journalists pressed Khanna on whether Hamas was justified to attack Israeli soldiers on Oct. 7, 2023. Khanna refused to agree. But Grim said those are the kinds of tough questions independent media are there to ask — and that American voters increasingly want to see their representatives in Congress answer. “People want to see you being accountable to questions, and if they don't agree with you, sometimes that's fine,” he said. “I think the smarter politicians are starting to recognize that.” ___ This story has been updated to correct Farah Berent's job to physician assistant, not teacher. ___ Associated Press writer Joey Cappelletti in Grand Rapids, Mich., contributed to this report.

article_text: A young fan allegedly raped by a British YouTuber and musician after a gig was an enthusiastic and willing participant when the sex started, a court has been told. Rapper Yung Filly, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, is fighting six charges of sexually penetrating a 20-year-old woman without consent in a Perth hotel room in September 2024. The 30-year-old also denies impeding the woman's breathing by applying pressure to her neck and three counts of assault occasioning bodily harm. Prosecutors say he bit, hit, choked and raped the woman after the pair had consensual sex, leaving her with significant bruising and visible bite marks on her skin. In closing submissions, defence lawyer David Edwardson KC said the woman went to the hotel "of her own free will", and she was happy to have sex with Barrientos. "She was an enthusiastic and willing participant when the sex act started," Mr Edwardson told the West Australian District Court jury on Tuesday. Mr Edwardson attacked prosecution claims the woman had been a victim of a powerful man, who took her phone away and didn't ask her if she wanted to have sex. "This notion of a so-called power imbalance ... this notion he somehow had a responsibility to ask her before each sex act performed … is nonsense," he said. "She was an adult, and she was perfectly capable of making her own decisions about what she would and wouldn't do." The prosecution case was problematic, and the evidence does not support the charges, Mr Edwardson said. "When you strip this case back to its basics, the state case rises and falls on the reliability of the complainant," he said. "We say (the woman's) evidence is riddled with inconsistencies, embellishments and outright lies." Mr Edwardson was also critical of the prosecution's expert medical evidence, saying it failed to establish the woman was sexually assaulted. He said it was incomplete and could not rule out that the significant bruising suffered by the woman was caused by "love bites" and not slapping and choking. The police investigation was also a deeply troubling feature of the case, Mr Edwardson said. "It has nothing to do with (the woman); it is about what the state chose not to find," he said. Investigators failed to follow up key evidence, such as who the woman was calling as she left the hotel, as recorded on CCTV. Mr Edwardson also questioned why police had not taken a statement from the Uber driver who took her home, and the woman's missing phone call evidence. The alleged victim also didn't mention being raped in the hours after the incident, he said. A series of videos she recorded only mentioned the rapper biting her, which he has admitted to during the trial. Prosecutor Danielle Clarke framed Barrientos as an "entitled man" with a "moderate degree of fame", who was sexually violent towards an impressionable young woman. "She meant nothing to him," she said. "What could have been and should have been consensual sex quickly escalated into sexual violence and a non-consensual nightmare." Ms Clarke said the woman consented to going back to the entertainer's hotel room but that did not mean "she was going to do anything that the accused wanted". "When you consider the little time he spent with her ... before he started biting, slapping and strangling her ... the state says he simply did not care," Ms Clarke said. "It did not matter what she was wearing or how famous, important or entitled (Barrientos) perceived himself to be. "Everyone has the right to say no, and she certainly did not want to engage in sexual acts with him that involved violence and brutality." Ms Clarke cast the woman as an open and honest witness. But Barrientos had been evasive, unresponsive and tried to hide behind the term "love bite" as a means of explaining the injuries the complainant allegedly suffered, she said. 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732) National Sexual Abuse and Redress Support Service 1800 211 028 Australian Associated Press

article_text: Teen killer appears to boast about murder in rap video filmed inside prison , 19, was given a life sentence last week after being found guilty of killing the 16-year-old on a North Ayrshire beach in 2025 A teenager convicted of murdering Kayden Moy has shared footage online from behind bars seemingly bragging about the killing. Jay Stewart, 19, received a life sentence last week following his conviction for the murder of the 16 year old on a North Ayrshire beach in 2025. The two-minute mobile phone clip was recorded inside a cell at HMP Polmont, showing Stewart with a t-shirt covering his face while rapping about the murder, and seemingly threatening additional violence following his eventual release. Responding to the footage on Thursday, Kayden's father Paul stated: "Today my family was devastated by a leaked video from inside Polmont showing Jay Stewart convicted of killing my son singing, laughing, and appearing to boast about taking my son's life. "Nothing will ever prepare a parent for something like this. "We live every day with the heartbreak of losing Kayden while the person responsible appears to show no remorse and no respect." The clip was recorded on a phone held by another prisoner, who can be heard laughing and cheering at several moments. The profanity-filled verses contain numerous references to the killing of "KM" or "Kayden". He also seemingly threatens additional violence upon release, stating at one point: "Everyone knows my scheme is violent, big plan for future ahead." Stewart and Cole Turley, 18, both received minimum 16-year prison sentences for the murder, while a 15 year old boy was imprisoned for a minimum of 14 years. Kayden suffered fatal stab wounds on Irvine beach on May 17. On the day of the incident, the teenagers travelled by train to Irvine, carrying a lock-back knife and a cosh concealed within clothing and a rucksack. After an initial altercation at the beach, the teenagers pursued Kayden, inflicting the fatal wound after he stumbled and fell to the ground. Subsequently, they were filmed on camera seemingly celebrating the attack. A Scottish Prison Service spokesperson said: "We understand the lasting impact this kind of offending has on families and the significant distress such videos can cause. "Our staff work hard to keep prisons safe and secure, using all available technology and intelligence to prevent illicit items, including mobile phones, entering our establishments. "While we do not comment on individuals, we continue to work with Police Scotland, and other partners, to take action against those who attempt to breach our security." A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Inquiries are ongoing following a report of an online communication offence from HM YOI Polmont on Tuesday July 28 2026."

article_text: China has taken a major step toward developing its first commercial fusion reactor by completing tests of the world's largest superconducting magnet. Weighing 582 tonnes, the device is designed to confine plasma at temperatures exceeding 100 million°C – conditions that replicate the processes taking place inside stars. The achievement brings China closer to its goal of demonstrating practical fusion power by 2030 while intensifying global competition in the race for virtually limitless clean energy. Built as part of the CRAFT project, the new toroidal superconducting magnet measures 21 meters in length. Its primary role is to generate an extremely powerful magnetic field capable of stabilizing superheated plasma and keeping it suspended at the center of a fusion reactor without allowing it to touch the reactor walls. Any contact between plasma and the vessel would instantly destroy conventional materials because temperatures inside a tokamak exceed 100 million°C. Chinese engineers report that the new system stores roughly three times more energy than the magnetic systems developed for the international ITER project while offering a magnetic volume approximately 1.3 times larger. China also achieved full domestic production of the system, manufacturing every key component-including specialized steel and superconducting materials-within the country. "Working at these scales and temperatures demands extraordinary precision in materials science. Developing superconductors that retain their properties under such extreme conditions effectively solves around 80 percent of the engineering challenges associated with fusion energy," physicist Dmitry Lapshin said in an interview with Pravda.Ru. The next phase of the CRAFT program will focus on assembling the complete experimental reactor. Construction is scheduled for completion in 2027, with the first demonstration of practical fusion power expected around 2030. China occupies a unique position in global fusion research. While remaining one of the seven principal partners in the international ITER program, Beijing is simultaneously developing its own independent projects, including EAST, CRAFT, BEST, and CFETR. Since joining ITER in 2007, China has manufactured 18 critical systems for the international reactor and incorporated the technological expertise gained into its domestic fusion industry. Observers attribute China's faster progress largely to centralized project management and funding. Unlike ITER, which coordinates contributions from multiple governments, the CRAFT project receives direct state financing estimated at approximately 6.3 billion yuan, allowing engineering decisions to move forward more rapidly. As a result, China's fusion program is widely considered to be progressing five to seven years ahead of the international schedule. While ITER aims to demonstrate a net energy gain from fusion reactions, China's BEST and CFETR projects focus on developing reactors capable of generating electricity for the power grid while producing their own tritium fuel. Modern fusion research continues to build upon the tokamak concept originally developed by Soviet scientists. Today, Russia remains one of ITER's major technological contributors, supplying approximately 9.1 percent of the project's in-kind contributions. In June 2026, the Kurchatov Institute and ITER signed a new cooperation agreement to continue their collaboration. Russian research institutes-including the Budker Institute of Nuclear Physics, NIIEFA, and VNIINM-are developing 25 highly specialized systems for ITER. These include high-power gyrotrons manufactured by Gikom for plasma heating, advanced niobium-tin superconducting conductors, and a massive 200-ton magnetic coil produced by the Sredne-Nevsky Shipyard that has already been installed at the reactor site in France. Russian scientists are also working on advanced tungsten-based materials for the reactor's first wall following ITER's transition away from beryllium. These ultra-high-temperature materials are expected to improve durability under the extreme conditions generated during sustained fusion reactions. The development of commercial fusion power demands breakthroughs across plasma physics, superconductivity, electromagnetism, and advanced materials science. As countries compete to build increasingly powerful magnetic confinement systems, fusion energy continues to attract attention as one of the most promising long-term sources of clean, low-carbon electricity. article_text: Meadowlands Racetrack hosted leg three of the New Jersey Sire Stakes for two-year-olds of each sex and gait on Friday, July 31. Platinum division races went for a purse of $35,211 while Silver dashes were contested for $14,085. Wall Of Fame, a product of Walner-Saadet, remained perfect in three Platinum-level filly trots for the driver and trainer, husband and wife team of Andy and Julie Miller, and stamped herself as one of the major players in the six-figure final, which takes place on Hambletonian Day, Aug. 8. Racing in the four-hole down the backstretch, Wall Of Fame vacated the rail at the five-eighths, made up ground on leader Loves Passion (Dexter Dunn) nearing the far turn, had to swerve into the three-lane when Dandelion Wine (Ake Svanstedt) popped out of the pocket for the stretch drive, but continued to gain through the lane – after a slight stall – before going on to half-length win over Dandelion Wine. Dejeuner (Andy McCarthy) rounded out the top three. “We’re just taking it race-by-race for now,” said Andy Miller. “She was kind of staying alongside [Dandelion Wine through the stretch], but when I hollered at her, she got going again. She’ll be in the Sire Stakes final next week and then we’ll decide from there [what we are going to do].” As the 1-9 favourite, Wall Of Fame returned $2.20 to win after completing the mile in 1:52.3. A $83,333 Lexington Select Yearling Sale purchase, the filly is owned by Andy Miller Stable of Cream Ridge, New Jersey, Jean Goehlen of Franconia, New Hampshire, Hutchison Harness of North Ridgeville, Ohio and Rick Huffman of Sigourney, Iowa. She paid $5.80 as the 9-5 second choice. Yannick Gingras drove the Walner-Ramona Hill filly, a $352,113 yearling purchase from the Standardbred Horse Sale, for trainer Ron Burke and owners Burke Racing Stable of Fredericktown, Pennsylvania, Crawford Farms Racing of Syracuse, New York, Brad Grant of Milton, Ont., and Lawrence Karr of Boca Raton, Florida. Wrong Sounds Right recorded his second victory in three tries after taking a split for Platinum-level colts and geldings on the trot for driver Todd McCarthy, trainer Jim Campbell and owner Runthetable Stables of Montvale, New Jersey. The homebred colt by Tactical Landing-Broadway Jo Ell used a wicked brush onto and around the far turn to challenge leader Lifetime Dreamer (Ake Svanstedt) and was strong through the stretch to record a one-length score over Presidente (Scott Zeron) in a lifetime-best 1:53. Mats (Yannick Gingras), the odds-on favourite, finished third. “He’s come along very nicely,” said Todd McCarthy. “We’re really happy with him. Aintmyfirstro Deo in now undefeated in three Platinum tilts for male pacers after leading wire-to-wire in a career-best 1:52 non-betting division. Driven by Scott Zeron for trainer Megan Scan, the Perfect Sting-Some Renditions gelding held off pocket-pursuer Velvet Ditch (Tim Tetrick) by half a length while We Want Eazy (Todd McCarthy) completed the field. Another winner for owner Hutchison Harness, Aintmyfirstro Deo surpassed his $37,500 Lexington price tag in his third successful start. In the Platinum filly pace, Perfect Hope Deo outsprinted Perfect Body (Brett Beckwith) to win by a head in 1:52 and break her maiden in her third start for driver Andy McCarthy and trainer Noel Daley. Sterl The Pearl (Joe Bongiorno) finished a length behind in third. The winner paid $12.60 as the 5-1 fourth choice in the betting. article_text: Former Stockdale ISD teacher sentenced to 13 years for improper relationship with student WILSON COUNTY, Texas — A former Stockdale Independent School District teacher has been sentenced to 13 years in prison after pleading no contest to charges stemming from an improper relationship with a student. Peter Aaron Leach was sentenced Thursday after waiving his right to a jury trial and entering no contest pleas to improper relationship between educator and student and indecency with a child by contact, both second-degree felonies. RELATED: Stockdale ISD teacher arrested after allegedly having inappropriate relations with student Leach also entered open pleas to child grooming and tampering with physical evidence, leaving the punishment for those charges up to the court. During sentencing, the court heard testimony from the victim, reviewed a sex offender evaluation, considered testimony from Leach's sex offender treatment counselor and examined a presentence investigation prepared by Wilson County Community Supervision Officer Taylor Harbour. The judge sentenced Leach to 13 years in prison for the improper relationship and indecency convictions, along with 10 years for the child grooming and evidence tampering convictions. All of the sentences will be served at the same time. Prosecutors had asked the court to impose the maximum 15-year sentence allowed under the plea agreement, while the defense requested deferred adjudication community supervision. According to the sex offender evaluation presented during the case, Leach's actions "single-handedly assisted in destroying the trust of students, faculty, families, and the public in the teaching community."

The notice of claim, which is a precursor to a possible lawsuit, is addressed to Sheriff Chris Nanos and a detective. It alleges wrongful arrest and property damage. Carlos Palazuelos, one of the men named in the claim, was detained Feb. 10 for questioning and released later without any charges as authorities searched for who kidnapped Guthrie, the mother of “TODAY” co-anchor Savannah Guthrie, earlier that month. The same day, the other man, Daniel Maddox, was placed in handcuffs at the home that was searched and held for several hours, the notice says. It also names his mother, who owns the home and alleges damage to the property. The notice, dated Monday and obtained by NBC affiliate KVOA of Tucson, says that deputies “arrested Carlos at gunpoint and held him without probable cause for approximately seven to eight hours” and that the arrest was made in a public fashion. The notice of claim, which KVOA reported has been filed, says that Palazuelos is innocent and that his home was “ransacked.” It alleges physical, emotional and reputational harm. It also says that Nanos posted on social media that a person had been arrested and that “the subject is currently being questioned in connection to the Nancy Guthrie investigation.” That post, in conjunction with statements from the sheriff’s office, made Palazuelos look like a suspect to the world, the notice says. “Despite requests by undersigned counsel, Sheriff Nanos and the PCSD have refused to retract their statements or to make clear that Carlos is innocent and had no involvement in the Guthrie case,” the notice says. The sheriff’s department said it does not commend on pending litigation. “The sheriff has said in multiple interviews that no one has been cleared in this case,” the office said. “This is an ongoing and active investigation.” Nanos said in an interview Friday on NBC News’ “Stay Tuned Now” that a judge signed off on the search warrant. “I can’t speak to ongoing litigation, but I can say this. I’m going to give you that warrant, that search warrant,’ Nanos said. “We went, we served the search warrant, we spoke to the individuals involved, and we keep moving forward with the investigation,” Nanos said. A man who identified himself as Palazuelos, a delivery driver, spoke to Telemundo outside the home in Rio Rico, around 60 miles south of Tucson, the time. Maddox was held “under guard” at a van for several hours, the notice says. The home is owned by Maddox’s mother, Josefina Maddox, who is also named in the notice. article_text: Monterey County flock cameras vandalized amid privacy debate Recent vandalism of flock cameras in Monterey County has sparked renewed discussions about privacy, surveillance, and public safety. Flock cameras in Monterey County have been targeted in recent acts of vandalism, reigniting debates over privacy, surveillance, and safety. In Seaside, two cameras were reportedly cut down along Del Monte Boulevard near the Home Depot parking lot. In another incident, a man allegedly rammed his vehicle into a camera to destroy it. “There’s more than just vandalism alone. I’m sure people have seen on the internet that this is kind of a trend, so we’re looking at possible conspiracy to commit a crime beyond the vandalism, and also those flock cameras are computer systems, so it’s denying access to a computer system, which is a felony in California,” Seaside police said. On Tuesday, the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office announced the arrest of a Pismo Beach man accused of destroying three flock license plate readers, one of which was captured on video. “Right now, my detectives are investigating the reason why he did it. Is there any motivations? Is he connected to other crimes that may have occurred into the area?” Monterey County Sheriff, Tina Nieto said. Detectives reported that the vandalism caused thousands of dollars in damages. Across the nation, there has been growing opposition to mass surveillance. “What we’re seeing with the public is pushback and outcry against this mass surveillance, this warrantless mass surveillance. So some people are taking action. I’m not going to encourage it, but what we have to be concerned about is an ongoing assault on our civil liberty,” Monterey County criminal defense attorney Chris Cain said. Cain also highlighted constitutional concerns regarding the cameras. “Flock cameras are more than just traffic cameras. It’s actually warrantless searches and mass surveillance on everyone. It records a lot more than just the license plate. It will record data for where a person is going, where they’ve been, and increasingly it’s recording facial recognition,” Cain said. Law enforcement officials maintain that the cameras are essential tools for solving crimes. “Whenever you take away what we call an ALPR system, any camera system, you’re taking away a tool that our investigators are using to help solve other crimes,” Nieto said. Flock Safety issued a statement, saying in part: “These are tools agencies rely on to respond quickly and help keep people safe. People have every right to make their voices heard, but criminal acts should never be part of that process.” Cain also raised concerns about the security of the camera systems, questioning whether Flock has adequate internal security measures to prevent data breaches or the sharing of information with third parties.

article_text: North Korea has installed screens around its building inside the inter-Korean truce village of Panmunjom to block it from public view, apparently for ongoing renovation work, military sources said Monday. The screens covering the Panmungak facility, located on the northern side of the Joint Security Area, were erected in April in what appeared to be part of renovation efforts, military sources with knowledge of the matter said. The North had put up screens around the building for renovation work in the past. Panmungak, built in 1969, sits 80 meters north of the Military Demarcation Line within the Demilitarized Zone separating the two Koreas. It directly faces South Korea's Freedom House in the JSA. The three-story Panmungak houses a guard command post and has the "pink phone," a direct hotline between the North and the United Nations Command, which administers the Armistice Agreement that halted the 1950-53 Korean War. The building has also served as a venue for key inter-Korean engagements in the past, including the 2018 summit between then President Moon Jae-in and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. The place made headlines as Kim emerged from Panmungak to meet Moon at the border line. Pyongyang has severed ties with Seoul since peace talks with the United States during the Moon administration collapsed without a deal. The regime declared in late 2023 that the two Koreas were "two hostile states." (Yonhap)

article_text: AYRSHIRE'S four MPs have urged the Scottish Government to pass on business rates reductions announced by the UK Government to pubs, social clubs and live music venues across Scotland. In a joint letter to Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth, they called for the Scottish Government to match both the 15 per cent business rates reduction introduced in England this year and the further 20 per cent reduction announced by Prime Minister Andy Burnham from April 2027. The MP's - Central Ayrshire's Alan Gemmell, North Ayrshire & Arran's Irene Campbell, Ayr Carrick and Cumnock's Elaine Stewart and Kilmarnock and Loudoun's Lillian Jones - joined 22 other Labour members in the plea. They warned that Scotland's hospitality sector had fallen around £200 million behind England in state support while pubs continue to close at an alarming rate. Central Ayrshire MP Mr Gemmell said: "Our pubs, clubs and live music venues are at the heart of communities across our towns and villages, and Scotland more broadly. "They're places where people meet, celebrate and support local musicians, while providing jobs and driving our local economy. "These businesses have faced years of rising costs, and the UK Labour Government has stepped in with meaningful business rates support. "I want businesses in Central Ayrshire to benefit from exactly the same support as businesses elsewhere in the UK. "There is no reason local venues should be left at a disadvantage because the Scottish Government chooses not to pass these savings on." The letter asks the Deputy First Minister to confirm that the Scottish Government will match both business rates reductions in full and meet with the MPs to discuss the importance of the decision for hospitality businesses across Scotland. article_text: The man accused of intentionally running over and killing boxer Hannah Rapp has reportedly been issued bonds set at more than $1 million. According to a Tuesday, July 28, report by CBS affiliate KBTX, Charles Medina, 31, appeared in a Texas hearing that morning where a judge set bonds for his “current case and … charges he was already out on bond for” in light of the July 18 death of Rapp. Bonds reportedly totaled $1,229,000. Us has reached out to Medina’s lawyer for comment. The outlet broke down each individual bond’s amount, with $500,000 set for “aggravated assault with a deadly weapon” and $250,000 set for “manslaughter” in relation to Rapp’s death after she was hit while riding her bike in College Station, Texas. She was 26 years old. An additional bond for “criminal mischief” was set at $25,000 and dated Tuesday, July 21 — the day Medina was arrested — while another bond for $250,000 was set for “deadly conduct – bond revocation” without a disclosed date. Two other bonds stemmed from alleged historic charges: “evading arrest” on March 17, 2025, and “deadly conduct” on February 14, 2024. According to the outlet, Medina’s legal team had requested that their client be issued bonds set at “$50,000 on each of his charges,” with Medina’s attorney, Sarah Wilkinson, stating in court that the bonds set “were excessive.” Medina is accused of fatally striking Rapp after passing two cyclists on the morning of her death before stopping, reversing and striking one of them, later identified as Rapp, who died at a local hospital. Local outlets reported at the time that Rapp had been riding alongside her boyfriend, Will Pollalis. In the wake of the incident, Brazos County Sheriff’s Office issued a Facebook statement. “On Saturday, July 18, 2026, just before 10:00 a.m., deputies with the Brazos County Sheriff’s Office were dispatched to the 2300 block of FM 150 in reference to a major crash involving a vehicle and a bicyclist,” it read. “Initial reports indicated that a vehicle had struck a bicyclist, leaving an adult female lying in the roadway. First responders arrived on scene and provided emergency medical care before the victim was transported to a local hospital. Despite lifesaving efforts, she later passed away at the hospital.” Us reported on the day of Medina’s arrest that he had a history of legal troubles due to alleged activity while driving. Jail records reviewed at the time showed that Medina was first arrested for reckless driving and evading arrest behind the wheel in 2012. He pled guilty to both counts. He was later arrested again in 2014 for reckless driving, then again for his alleged involvement in a hit-and-run in 2020. During Tuesday’s hearing, the judge stated that Medina is a danger to “himself, his family, the public, and law enforcement,” per the outlet. His manslaughter charge will reportedly see a status hearing in 60 days, however the charge “is subject to change once the investigation is over.”

article_text: China's ethnic unity law is the latest attempt to erase its minorities Wind blows across the grassy steppes as the Great Wall looms long in the distance, marking the ancient barrier between Mongolia and China. Gone are the days when its stones would shake with the thundering hoof-beats of Mongol hordes. The nomadic horsemen have been displaced from their pastures into city apartments in the Chinese Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Even their written language, preserved from the Russian influence overwriting it in Mongolia, is at risk of slipping away, like so much of their way of life already has. Ethnic unity On July 2, in New York City, Tibetan man Lobga Rangzen approached the United Nations headquarters and set himself on fire in an act of political protest. Amnesty International said the 52-year-old's self-immolation was in response to China's new ethnic unity law, which has sparked fears ethnic groups could face extinction. The law was designed to create a "shared" national identity among China's 56 ethnic groups. Amnesty International's deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks, said the incident was a moment to reflect on the human cost of certain policies. "A law that brazenly pushes non-Han ethnic groups including Tibetans, Uyghurs and Mongolians toward a single, state-defined national identity rather than protecting their distinct cultures and languages," Ms Brooks said. An article by China's state news agency, Xinhua, shared by the Chinese Ministry of Justice, said the law stipulated that "upholding national unity and ethnic solidarity is the responsibility of all Chinese citizens, and prohibits discrimination and suppression against any ethnic group". "It also combats violent terrorism, ethnic separatism and religious extremism, holding organisers, planners, perpetrators, instigators and funders of these activities criminally liable." Fifty-six races under one red flag The Han Chinese are China's largest and most dominant ethnic group, accounting for 17 per cent of the world's population. But 125 million Chinese citizens belong to 55 non-Han ethnic groups, including the Zhuang, Uyghur, Hui, Manchu, Yi, Tibetans and Mongolians. Parts of China's history were dominated by non-Han Dynasties: the Manchu Qing (1644–1912) and the Mongol Yuan (1271–1368). Enghebatu Togochog, director of the Southern Mongolian Human Rights Centre, said Mongols living through the Qing Dynasty enjoyed greater rights under the ruling Manchus. "Mongolians were always treated as pretty much the co-ruler of the Empire," Mr Togochog said. During this dynasty, Mongolia was a country under China's political influence, made up of a northern region (Outer Mongolia) and a more populous southern region (Inner Mongolia). Today, the northern region is the independent nation of Mongolia, while the southern territory remains part of China as the Inner Mongolian Autonomous Region. An empire divided The Chinese government insists the new laws are not being implemented to suppress ethnic groups or languages, but to prevent separatism. Following the 1911 revolution in which the Manchu Qing dynasty was overthrown, Mongolia, followed shortly afterwards by Tibet, declared independence from China. Outer Mongolia became a communist nation in the 1920s, remaining so until the fall of the Soviet Union in the 1990s. Inner Mongolia has remained a part of China, while the independent state of Tibet was annexed by the Chinese in 1951. During World War II, Mao Tse-Tung, founder of the People's Republic of China, called on "the nation of Inner Mongolia" to join him in resisting the Japanese and recognised it as a nation. "We feel that the people of Inner Mongolia have the right to solve all their internal problems, and no one has the authority to interfere by force in their living, habits, religion, ethics, and all other right," Chairman Mao said. "It may, according to the principle of self-determination, organise its own life and form its own government." The Japanese established a puppet government in parts of Inner Mongolia, but the state — called Mengjiang — ceased to exist after the Japanese surrender. Head of China Investigations at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, Bethany Allen, said the new unity policies were driven by Chinese President Xi Jinping's obsession with control. "It's harder for the Chinese government to inject propaganda into those communities and to surveil and control what those communities are saying and thinking," Ms Allen said. Life under Communist China Initially, Inner Mongolia was organised into an autonomous region with greater political rights. What followed was decades of persecution. Mr Togochog said government crackdowns started in the 1950s, when tens of thousands of Mongolian elites were accused of being national separatists, suffering politic persecution and imprisonment. This was just a taste of what came when Chairman Mao declared his decade-long "Cultural Revolution", which saw the destruction of cultural artefacts, societal upheaval and the persecution, imprisonment or death of millions. According to a study published by the University of Cambridge, more than 16,000 Mongols were killed and five times that many were maimed. Mr Togochog said the Mongolian population was "completely devastated by this large-scale genocide campaign". According to a 2020 census, Mongols have now become a minority within Inner Mongolia, representing just 18 per cent of the total population. End of the nomads Amnesty international's Tibetan advocate, Kyinzom Dhongdue, said the new ethnic unity law "unambiguously promotes and reinforces China's long-running policies that have already devastated the rights of Uyghurs, Tibetans and other non-Han ethnic groups". "The Chinese government is pursuing a long-term project of forced assimilation. Or, as described by Tibetans, a cultural genocide. "It seeks to fundamentally reshape how Tibetans, Uyghurs and other peoples, including Southern Mongolians speak, learn, worship and, ultimately, understand who they are." Ms Allen said Chinese President Xi Jinping was pushing China towards a sort of monoculture. "The very heavy-handed push towards assimilation should be seen through the lens of control and Xi Jinping's paranoia." Mr Togochog said the Mongol way of life has disappeared, despite resistance from pastoralists, herders and students. "Starting in the 2000s, the Chinese government targeted Mongolian way of life. They resettled all the nomads and herders from their ancestral lands to Chinese populated urban areas," he said. "Their livestock were just forced to be raised in fences, we were not allowed to practice our own, traditional, way of life." In 2015, the government publicly announced the last remaining nomads in China had been resettled, ending a way of life for Mongols, Tibetans, Uyghurs and Kazaks that had stretched back thousands of years. 'We've already lost everything' In 2020, protests rocked the region of Inner Mongolia after the Chinese government ordered an end to Mongolian-language classes for first-year primary students, in favour of Mandarin. Authorities also began a region-wide censorship campaign, shutting down Mongolian WeChat groups and removing Mongolian-language books from the shelves of retail outlets. "Southern Mongolians know that this is the last chance to stand as Mongolian People … if you lose your language, you lose everything," Mr Togochog said. "What is remaining is the language, that's the last defence of the Mongolian national identity … what we call the 'final solution' to the Mongolia question." Mr Togochog said between 8,000 and 10,000 Mongols were arrested and detained during the protests. Ms Allen said Premier Xi wanted to eliminate "ingroup loyalty" among ethnic groups like the Mongols with the new law. "This is nothing but cultural genocide … they want to make you directly Chinese," Mr Togochog said. Ms Allen said the new laws made her "really sad" and she said for many of the ethnic groups inside China, there was no diaspora for them to look to for cultural and linguistic preservation. "I think it's such a shame for China to be heading in this direction when many other similarly situated countries are working very, very hard to preserve and revive their minority languages."
